Question: When can I retire as an expat, and what are the biggest expat retirement mistakes?
Answer: When you can retire as an expat depends on how much you have now, how much you need, and what you are investing in. If you have a mixed portfolio of stocks and bonds, you can withdraw 3%- 4% per year, depending on how long you want your retirement to last. (Source, Quora and MyMoneyDesign). If you are in cash, you can’t withdraw more than 3%, as inflation will erode the money. So, having too much money in cash is the first mistake. Apart from that, the three biggest mistakes are: 1. Not factoring in currency risks When I started travelling in 2007, the Pound was 2:1 against the USD, and many British ex-pats relied on that to last forever, which it didn't. The South African Rand and many currencies have fared far worse. This especially affects expats who have a specific income. 2. Not factoring in indirect costs like the hassles of owning certain assets If you rely on rental income as an expat, you face the previous risk - currency risks. What you might not be factoring in is hassles. As a 75-year-old, do you want to chase up tenants to pay? 3. Tax risks and complexity Linked to the second point, having numerous assets, such as properties in many locations, can be a hassle. It can also increase tax risks and complexity. Depending on your situation, a simpler solution can often make sense, like owning one house and having one or two simple portfolios.

Answer: Imagine you go to a steak restaurant today. Would you say we shouldn't eat there as we are paying the steak restaurant's mortgage or bills? Of course not. They are providing a service. Whether it is worth the cost versus cooking yourself is another question. The same is valid for renting. You might say it isn’t strictly the same, which, of course, is true. However, what is the same is you are paying for a service. The landlord is: As a result, you can use the money to invest in other assets and save time and hassles. Simple example. Imagine somebody would have spent $100,000 on a housing deposit in 1990. That would now be worth well over $1.1m + if you would have invested in indexes like the Dow Jones and S&P500, provided you reinvested the dividends. Most property markets haven't appreciated that much. So, it isn’t as simple as saying rent is more expensive because you are building up equity in the home. There are opportunity costs associated with housing. If you run your own business and it is in “growth mode”, that 100k reinvested into your business could be an indirect $5m-$10m loss in the future. If I had used the money to buy a property in 2018 or 2019, I would have literally (indirectly) lost a fortune. That doesn’t mean you should never buy, but it is why you have many rent vs buy calculators. The issue is that apart from economists and a few others, few people consider all the variables.

Question: What are the benefits and risks of investing in stocks of companies that mine for precious metals like gold and silver?
Answer: Gold and silver mining companies aren’t always linked to the metal's price, even if there can be a correlation. Some private companies, say private equity, raise money to extract gold and silver. Those projects are high-risk and high-return. You could easily lose your capital or make 10x because the result depends on finding the gold. In terms of mining stocks listed on the global stock markets, the main risks are: -Revolutions -More taxes on mining companies -Renationalisations. Look at what has happened in Niger recently. It isn’t about gold and silver but shows the risks in the commodities business (Uranium in this case). And let’s not forget, like any individual stocks, you also face individual company risks. The CEO might make the wrong decisions, or the company might not innovate. That is a risk for all individual stocks in every industry versus buying a fund or ETF. Some investors buy mining stocks because they are uncorrelated with much of the general market. Mining and energy did well last year when the general stock markets fell. At other times, they significantly underperform.

Question: Do all rich people really deserve their money?
Answer: If we get into a subjective debate about “deserve” it becomes a pointless argument. In some religious societies, people would think that those engaged in gambling and alcohol businesses don’t deserve their money. Even in some Western societies, people find it questionable that some people can earn a lot from gambling businesses, adult entertainment and other legal services. Plenty of people, globally, think it is ridiculous that footballers can make a lot of money. YouGov, a UK polling agency, found that the public feel like top footballers should earn 75,000 Pounds a year (about $100,000) This is why we have markets, and personal choice. If not, it becomes a subjective debate about who deserves what.

Question: Is expensive wine worth it?
Answer: An incredible test was done on this. Frédéric Brochet, who was a PhD student at the time, dyed a white wine red and gave it to 54 wine “experts”. To cut a long story short, he told them he was showing them two different wines when in actual fact, he was showing them the same wine - he merely dyed one wine to a different colour. The research paper is called The Color of Odors. The research also shows that visual cues can sometimes override our senses of taste and smell. That is why so much time, effort and money is spent designing nice wine bottles and glasses. The same luxury wine wouldn’t taste as good because it wouldn’t release as many endorphins if it was served in a paper cup. We see the same thing with other products. In a study done a few years ago, participants were shown two cakes. One cost $15 and one $55. One looked nicer than the other in terms of decoration. Yet they were both the same….the researchers put a different price tag on the same cake and made the designs look nicer. People were shocked when they found out. Some insisted on trying them both again, saying the more expensive one tasted better! So, in answer to your question, a lot of this is marketing. Therefore, it isn’t worth spending loads on expensive wines and consumer products if it stops you from investing for retirement and gaining financial security. It isn’t like hotels or business class flights, where the benefits are clearer. That doesn’t mean you should never drink expensive wine if you like it, or it is linked to an experience like being invited to a good sporting event with friends. It merely means many things subconsciously affect our preceptions of quality and taste.

Question: Why don't people who invest in the stock market look at news in a constructive manner and evaluate said risks rather than panic at every single rumour and potential risk causing stock price to plummet?
Answer: It is an interesting question because these things go around in cycles. It isn’t just the significant events like the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, Brexit and Trump in 2016 or COVID-19 in 2020. Looking back, relatively minor events are always sensationalized as well. Who now can remember the 2011 Eurozone crisis? At the time, it was a big news story - Debt crisis sends financial markets into turmoil – Monday 8 August 2011 Or the so-called flash crash at a similar time? 2010 flash crash - Wikipedia During each event, markets have recovered or never crashed in the first place, often doing the opposite of what the media predicted. Markets in the UK hit record highs in 2018, barely two years after the Brexit vote. They didn’t crash in 2016 after Trump’s election or during the disputed US election in 2020. They recovered quickly after COVID-19, and the events mentioned above, such as the flash crash, are very forgettable. Yet, people still believe in the same narratives. The same people who worried about a US stock market crash (and the market never recovering) in 2016 and a disputed election in 2020 will likely worry about the outcome of the 2024 election! I guess it shows the power of storytelling.

Question: What insights can be gained from the rise and fall of the Vanderbilt family's net worth in terms of wealth creation, management, and preservation?
Answer: Did you know that CNN anchor Anderson Cooper is the son of Gloria Vanderbilt and was part of the first generation to not gain wealth without working for it? Interestingly, he speaks about that fact as if it were a blessing, not a curse. And he is probably right. To answer your question, historians who have examined the family have said they didn't focus on building generational wealth. They focused on spending more than everybody else and did not manage risk, even though events like world wars could always be around the corner. So, the critical lesson is that shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves in three generations is a real thing. Those that want to build generational wealth need to focus on structuring. For this reason, most ultra-wealthy families, such as royal families, have their money in trust. They don’t want the children or grandchildren to waste it in one go. These days, it isn’t just the ultra-wealthy who create trusts for this reason.

Question: Why would a person want to set up a trust?
Answer: Imagine you are a wealthy person in Egypt and Tunisia. Things have been working well in your business for decades. Then the Arab Spring happens: One thing leads to another, and you lose your business. I also saw several people lose their businesses due to the indirect effects of the 2014 Thailand coup. A trust can separate you from your assets, like how a limited liability company is a separate legal entity from an individual. That isn’t to mention the potential tax benefits in some countries, and ease of passing on assets.

Question: How do you invest as an expat if you do not know where you will eventually settle?
Answer: I have been an expat for close to twelve years. Here I am looking younger and fresher (with more hair, too!) more than over a decade ago, as a new expat in China. Where you live now is largely irrelevant to your investments. Sure, some things make a difference. For example, there are tax implications if you live in the US as an expat. But in general, there are loads of expat-focused accounts, which are designed to be flexible, that are portable, and move with you when you move to another location. Often all you need to do is update your credit/debit card payment or send it from a new bank account. What matters is what you invest in. The best way to invest, according to a lot of academic research, is: If somebody worth an estimated $ 400 million can’t do it, then very few people (if any) can. So, ultimately, most do-it-yourself (DIY) investors, whether expats or non-expats, fail for the same reasons. They don’t understand risk - they either take none and lose to inflation in the bank or get seduced by get rich quick scheme. Expats merely have more challenges. One of the critical challenges these days is the “death” of the lifetime expat. No longer are expats having just one assignment. Often expats are being moved around every 3–4 years. The coronavirus has only exaggerated that process, with many expats being unexpectedly moved on. So, an portable online solution that can be “taken with you” when you move is essential. As a final comment, it is essential to remember that staying in cash isn’t a safe option. Look how much the Euro, British Pound and many other currencies have lost in recent years.
